steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Scene understanding has been a problem in robot perception for a long time. In the last decade, SLAM systems have moved from building only geometric representations for localization, to semantic and interpretable representations that can be used for interaction. Semantic SLAM and object-based perception have advanced a lot, and this was powered by progress in the machine learning and computer vision communities. More recently, 3D scene graphs have come up as a unifying representation that integrates structure and semantics. But these applications use fixed-class semantic models, and this limits how versatile these systems are.

Progress in LLM research offers a solution to this problem, because they can bridge the gap between visual and textual information thanks to their open vocabularies. Methods like CLIP and ViLD have been used to enrich 3D reconstructions with semantics, for example in OpenScene, ConceptFusion, and NLMap. These methods can identify objects and properties of the scene, and they can even do navigation using human instructions. However there are still open questions about how to integrate this capability into the modules of a robotic system. In particular, can the embedded semantic understanding be used for tasks like place recognition and localization?

- LEXIS (Language-EXtended Indoor SLAM): open-vocabulary LLM capabilities + classical localization and mapping
  - conventional approaches: separate models for room classification, place recognition, semantic understanding
  - ours: single pre-trained model does all of these efficiently
  - output: semantically segmented pose graph (Fig. 1)
- Contributions:
  - lightweight topological pose graph with CLIP features
  - online room segmentation from semantic features (different room sizes, layouts, open-floor plans)
  - place recognition -> hierarchical, room-aware loop closures
  - extensive evaluation (room segmentation/classification, place recognition, unified visual SLAM), standard + custom multi-floor datasets, planning demo

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Scene understanding has been a problem in robot perception for a long time. In the last decade, SLAM systems have moved from building only geometric representations for localization, to semantic and interpretable representations that can be used for interaction. Semantic SLAM and object-based perception have advanced a lot, and this was powered by progress in the machine learning and computer vision communities. More recently, 3D scene graphs have come up as a unifying representation that integrates structure and semantics. But these applications use fixed-class semantic models, and this limits how versatile these systems are.

Progress in LLM research offers a solution to this problem, because they can bridge the gap between visual and textual information thanks to their open vocabularies. Methods like CLIP and ViLD have been used to enrich 3D reconstructions with semantics, for example in OpenScene, ConceptFusion, and NLMap. These methods can identify objects and properties of the scene, and they can even do navigation using human instructions. However there are still open questions about how to integrate this capability into the modules of a robotic system. In particular, can the embedded semantic understanding be used for tasks like place recognition and localization?

In this work we combine the open-vocabulary capabilities of LLMs with classical localization and mapping methods, and we develop LEXIS (Language-EXtended Indoor SLAM). Conventional approaches use separate models for room classification, place recognition and semantic understanding, but our approach uses one single pre-trained model to do all of these functions efficiently. The output is a pose graph that is semantically segmented, as shown in Fig. 1. Our contributions are:

- A lightweight topological pose graph representation with CLIP features embedded in it.

- A method that uses semantic features to do online room segmentation, which can handle different room sizes, layouts and open-floor plans.

- A place recognition approach that builds on these room segmentations to propose hierarchical loop closures that are room-aware.

- An extensive evaluation of the system for indoor real-time room segmentation and classification, for place recognition, and as a unified visual SLAM system, using standard and custom multi-floor datasets, and a demonstration for planning tasks.

More recently, 3D scene graphs [3,4] have come up as a unifying representation that integrates structure and semantics [5,6]. But these applications use fixed-class semantic models, and this limits how versatile these systems are.

Progress in LLM research offers a solution to this problem, because they can bridge the gap between visual and textual information thanks to their open vocabularies. Methods like CLIP [7] and ViLD [8] have been used to enrich 3D reconstructions with semantics, for example in OpenScene [9], ConceptFusion [10], and NLMap [11]. These methods can identify objects and properties of the scene, and they can even do navigation using human instructions [12]. However there are still open questions about how to integrate this capability into the modules of a robotic system. In particular, can the embedded semantic understanding be used for tasks like place recognition and localization?

In this work we combine the open-vocabulary capabilities of LLMs with classical localization and mapping methods, and we develop LEXIS (Language-EXtended Indoor SLAM). Conventional approaches use separate models for room classification, place recognition and semantic understanding, but our approach uses one single pre-trained model to do all of these functions efficiently. - A lightweight topological pose graph representation with CLIP features embedded in it.

- A method that uses semantic features to do online room segmentation, which can handle different room sizes, layouts and open-floor plans.

- A place recognition approach that builds on these room segmentations to propose hierarchical loop closures that are room-aware.

- An extensive evaluation of the system for indoor real-time room segmentation and classification, for place recognition, and as a unified visual SLAM system, using standard and custom multi-floor datasets, and a demonstration for planning tasks.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Scene understanding is a long-standing problem in robot perception. Over the last decade, SLAM systems have shifted from building purely geometric representations for localization to semantic and interpretable representations for interaction [1,2]. Semantic SLAM and object-based perception have made significant advances, powered by progress in the machine learning and computer vision communities. More recently, 3D scene graphs [3,4] have emerged as a unifying representation to integrate structure and semantics [5,6]. However, the use of fixed-class semantic models in these applications limits the versatility of these systems.

The progress of LLM research offers a solution to this challenge, since they can bridge the gap between visual and textual information with their open vocabularies. Methods such as CLIP [7] and ViLD [8] have been used to enrich 3D reconstructions with semantics, as shown by methods such as OpenScene [9], ConceptFusion [10], and NLMap [11]. These methods can identify objects and scene properties, and can even carry out navigation using human instructions [12]. Yet open questions remain about integrating this capability into the modules of a robotic system. In particular, can embedded semantic understanding be harnessed for tasks such as place recognition and localization?

In this work, we combine the open-vocabulary capabilities of LLMs with classical localization and mapping methods to develop LEXIS (Language-EXtended Indoor SLAM). Unlike conventional approaches that employ separate models for room classification, place recognition and semantic understanding, our approach uses a single pre-trained model to execute all of these functions efficiently. The output is a semantically segmented pose graph, as shown in Fig. 1. Our specific contributions are:

- A lightweight topological pose graph representation embedded with CLIP features.

- A method to leverage semantic features for online room segmentation, able to accommodate different room sizes, layouts and open-floor plans.

- A place recognition approach that builds on these room segmentations to propose hierarchical, room-aware loop closures.

- Extensive evaluation of the system for indoor real-time room segmentation and classification, place recognition, and as a unified visual SLAM system, using standard and custom multi-floor datasets, with a demonstration for planning tasks.
